Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

 

Letting $\theta =2x,$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡2x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$

$$

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}+3,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-3{cos}^{2}⁡x+3{sin}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+{x}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+3x)\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\frac{(\pi /2)^{3}}{3}+3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}]-[-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )+\frac{(-\pi /2)^{3}}{3}+3(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{24}+\frac{3\pi }{2})-(-\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{24}-\frac{3\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{12}+3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

A region in the $xy$-plane is bounded by the curve $y=6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{2}.$ The area of the region is

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{2}$ is 

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))={sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2}).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{(x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)|}_{\pi /2}^{5\pi /2} \\  & =3[(\frac{5\pi }{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{2}))-(\frac{\pi }{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))] \\  & =3[(\frac{5\pi }{2}-1)-(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)] \\  & =3(2\pi ) \\  & =6\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
